## Phase 166 (executed 2026-07-29 — the adversarial-round cost question: what the rounds are actually buying, and the two authoring rules that would make them cheaper)

**The question, asked by Wade after Phase 165's round.** *"They seem like they're getting more costly than they used to be, I think they used to be one reviewer, are we getting good results for the added complexity or are we just arguing between more sessions?"* Docs-only phase; its whole product is a measurement, a portable rule pair, and a filed decision that the maintainer — not this session — resolves.

**The drift is real and was never decided — and the first draft of this paragraph got it wrong twice, which the round caught.** Re-derived from each phase's own `PHASE_LOG.md` round record rather than from `CLAUDE.md`'s one-liner index: 1 reviewer originally; **2** as the mode through Phase 152, but with at least **five** exceptions running 3 or 4 (126, 128, 138, 147, 149) rather than the two the first draft claimed; **3** as the mode from 153 onward — **not six consecutive**, because Phase 154's entry says outright *"Adversarial round: run — two reviewers (claims-and-coherence, test-quality)"*; and Phase 165 at **4**. The honest shape is a ragged series whose mode rose from 2 to 3, not a clean escalation. Nobody chose it.

**The cost, named — and flagged as unverifiable from this tree.** Phase 165's round spent **~910k sub-agent tokens**: 704.1k across four reviewers (156.7k / 178.5k / 187.0k / 181.9k — the rounded figures an earlier draft gave summed to 705k, which is a rounding artifact, not the total) plus 205.8k for two pre-phase scouts, at 12–37 minutes each, run in parallel. **These numbers come from the prior session's tool metadata and no artifact in the repo records them** — nor do the reviewer reports behind the overlap figure below exist anywhere in the tree. **That is precisely the deficiency Phase 164 was faulted for one phase earlier** (*"the five auditor reports were not preserved, so no per-lens FP rate is auditable"*), and this phase repeated it while measuring rigour. A later reader cannot check any of it, which is the strongest argument in this entry for the round-yield ledger filed below.

**They are not redundant, which is the part the worry gets wrong.** Overlap was roughly **15%**: of ~25 distinct findings only 3–4 were reached by more than one lens, and **each of the four lenses produced its sharpest finding alone** — fix-correctness found the PyYAML probe that renders a newly-prescribed remedy inert on the maintainer's own machine; guard-vacuity found the four ordinary authoring habits that walk through a line-scoped guard; record-truth found that the phase's *central framing* was false; the independent class re-sweep found a false sentence in the phase's own new script header and the guard's population hole. On findings-per-reviewer, four was efficient. So "are we just arguing between more sessions" answers **no** on the evidence.

**But the reason the yield stays high is not flattering, and it points at a cheaper intervention.** **Twelve of the sixteen phases from 150 to 165 had a round that found the phase's own guards vacuous or its mutation claim self-selected** — 150, 153, 154, 155, 156, 157, 158, 159, 160, 162, 163, 165 (thirteen log rows; 159 is logged as 159a and 159b). Two more are borderline and excluded with reason: Phase 151 killed all eleven of its mutations but *two only after repairing the tests that were supposed to kill them*, and Phase 152 ran a second mutation round whose survivor count I could not pin down from its entry. Excluded as a different class: 161 and 164, whose rounds found record falsehoods and a broken class sweep rather than weak guards.

**The first draft of that number said nine, and how it went wrong is the most useful thing in this phase.** It was derived by grepping `CLAUDE.md`'s Phase-log table — the **one-liner index** — instead of `PHASE_LOG.md`, where the round records actually live. The index rows are ~200-character summaries that mention survivor counts only when they happen to be the row's headline, so three unambiguous members were invisible to it: Phase **156**, whose reviewer ran 83 mutations and watched **28 survive** against the phase's own reported "33 of 33 killed"; Phase **162** (15 of 67 survived, 22%); and Phase **163** (25 of 65, **38% — recorded in its own entry as the highest survivor rate in the log**, which is to say the author was comparing across rounds and still did not fold it in). **That is rule 1's "where it looks" class, committed by the phase that ships rule 1, against its own headline number.** A second, smaller miscount preceded it: an earlier pass said *eight*, having grepped `vacuous|mutations surviving|survivors`, which catches 153/154's "guard survivors" but misses 159a's "self-selected … 8 more survived" and 159b's "surviving mutations". The first draft's account of that grep omitted the `survivors` term and so did not explain its own result — corrected here.

**The corrected number strengthens the argument and indicts the derivation.** Three quarters of the last sixteen phases shipped guards their own round found weak. **The rounds are working as a detector while the authoring step is not learning, and adding reviewers treats the symptom.** Splitting Phase 165's findings by what it took to reach them: about **half was author-side sloppiness catchable by inspection in minutes** — a past tense implying an incident that never happened, wrong arithmetic, a provenance claim one `git log --follow` refutes, a `grep` cited as evidence that the same commit invalidated, "verified correct" about sites never actually checked — and about **half needed independent execution against real state**, which no checklist reaches. Only the second half is what a reviewer is for.

**What shipped: the half that is clearly right.** `_shared/adversarial-review.md` gains § *Before you spawn anyone — the author-side pass* (consumed by **8 skills and 3 other `_shared/` partials**, so it ships to consumers rather than living in `tools/` — an earlier draft said *four* partials, having counted the file's own self-description at `:5` as a citation of itself; caught by the author-side pass). Two rules:

1. **A mutation set that only reverts the text a guard asserts proves nothing.** Deleting a phrase a guard requires goes red by construction — that tests string equality. Four of Phase 165's nine mutations were that shape while eight real bypasses stood. The rule directs mutation at the guard's **assumptions** instead, with the four classes that round found: *what it matches on* (a line-scoped guard loses to a backslash continuation, a flag named before the command, a variable, or a list step separating command from qualifier), *where it looks* (one guard excluded the installer — a file that already prescribed the script the guard was about), *what it accepts* (a substring check is satisfied by an incidental use of that substring, which marks a dangerous line compliant rather than merely missing it), and *when it runs* (prose asserting "rejected before anything is deleted" is not a test of the ordering). Report the fraction and name the survivors you decline to close: a hole named in the guard is maintenance, a hole found later is drift.
2. **Re-read your own new prose against the code it describes.** Both defects Phase 165's round found *in the fix itself* were sentences its author had just written that contradicted the file they sat in, both in the same wrong-scope class the fix existed to remove. New prose is the least-reviewed text in any change — no history, no reviewer has seen it, and its author is the one person who cannot read it cold — and its claims about *paths* are as easily wrong in the consumer's installed layout as in the author's.

The section closes on what the pass cannot do: it never executes the change against real state, which is where the findings you most need come from.

**What deliberately did not ship: the reviewer count.** The proposal — 2 reviewers, record-truth and class-completeness folded into the mandatory author-side pass, escalate to 3 only when a phase ships behaviour *and* a record making numeric claims — is filed under `## Decisions to revisit later` for Wade, not enacted. Two reasons. A reviewer-count policy is a judgement about cost tolerance that belongs to the person paying, and the evidence here is **one round's composition, not a measurement across rounds**. Recording it as ratified would be the same overreach this phase is about.

**The gap that would end the argument rather than re-run it:** there is no round-yield tracking anywhere. Phase 93 built a Tier-2b calibration ledger for `/test-audit`; nothing equivalent exists for rounds, so findings-per-reviewer over time cannot be computed and the count can only be tuned on anecdote. If it is going to be tuned, that ledger is the prerequisite — filed with the decision.

**Suite: 1874 passed, 4 skipped** (1871 + 3 guards for the new section).

**Adversarial round: RUN — two reviewers** (rule-soundness; evidence-audit on a different model), isolated worktrees, both given `9f17ddf`, both landing on its parent, both detecting it and reading through `git show`. Two rather than three by the policy this phase proposes: docs-only, no behaviour to execute. **It went badly, in the exact way the phase is about, and the phase's product is better for it.**

*The evidence lens* found the **central recurrence number undercounted (9 → 12 of 16)**, because it had been derived from `CLAUDE.md`'s one-liner index instead of `PHASE_LOG.md`'s round records — invisible to it were Phase 156 (28 of 83 survived against its own "33 of 33 killed"), 162 (15 of 67) and 163 (25 of 65, its entry calling it the highest survivor rate in the log). It also killed **"six consecutive"** (Phase 154's entry says *"two reviewers"* outright), corrected the **125–152 exception set from two to five** (126, 128, 138, 147, 149), caught the rounded token components summing to 705k against a stated 704k, and — the finding that stings most — that the **token and overlap figures are unverifiable from the tree while the record did not say so**, which is Phase 164's exact fault one phase later, in a phase about measuring rigour. All corrected above; the caveat is now in the entry.

*The rule-soundness lens* found four defects in the rule text itself. **Rule 1 was logically mis-scoped in both directions:** "a set that *only* reverts…" self-clears on the very set that motivated it (four of nine reverts is not *only*), while "mutate assumptions, **not** the content it checks" condemned the revert that is the *whole* test of a declared **reversion guard** — this repo ships ~97 of those — and condemned the population-emptying mutation that is the only possible test of a **vacuity guard**, a guard the preceding round had added on purpose. Rule 1 is now additive, with both carve-outs named. **"Name the survivors you decline to close" was an unbounded licence:** the preceding round's author had labelled that round's single biggest hole "known blind spot, as designed", and the round required it fixed — so a residual now has to be impossible to close *in kind*, and "an ordinary in-repo idiom reaches it" makes it a defect wearing a residual's label. **Two assumption classes were missing**, both produced by these same rounds: *over-strictness* (the guard that required a `bash ` prefix the repo's own house style omits) and *reachability*. And **the section had no invoker** — no skill cites it, `CLAUDE.md`'s gate paragraph enumerated the procedure without it, and its two plan-time readers (`/claim-task` Step 7, `/plan-review` Step 3) would have been told to mutation-test guards that do not exist yet. It is now role-bound, excludes the plan-time flow, and `CLAUDE.md`'s gate names it as a step.

**The two reviewers disagreed on the headline number, and the one that read the source of truth won.** The rule-soundness lens independently computed **10 of 17** — from `CLAUDE.md`'s index, reproducing the phase's own error one level up. The evidence lens read `PHASE_LOG.md`. Verified by hand: 12 of 16 phase numbers, 13 log rows. `§ Running more than one reviewer`'s "never weight findings by how many reviewers agree" earned its keep in the *disagreeing* direction here.

**The section shipped with zero guards, which is the finding that should have been embarrassing before a reviewer said it.** Deleting all ~3.2k characters left the whole suite green — in the one file that already has a purpose-built guard module, amended by Phase 154, whose own round explained why prose guards on this file are load-bearing. Worse, this phase inserted a **cost argument** into that guarded section and the existing hedge list could not see two ordinary paraphrased softenings of the multi-reviewer requirement (*"a single reviewer is often the right call"*), which is rule 1's own **"what it accepts"** class applied to the guard covering the file the phase was editing. Now: `author_pass_problems()` with 14 required rules including both carve-outs, the residual criterion and the counter-finding; five cost-framed patterns added to `_HEDGES`; softened twins for both. **+3 tests, 17 of 17 mutations killed** — and three of those mutations initially *survived* because the predicate used over-permissive alternations (`who this addresses|the *author*`, `cannot do|cannot catch`), the same defect class a third time, each found by mutating the predicate rather than reading it.

**The one-sidedness finding is worth naming separately** because it is a judgement error rather than a slip: the shipped section carried the cost argument (*"more reviewers is the expensive way to treat that"*) while the counter-finding — ~15% overlap, each lens producing its sharpest finding alone, findings-per-reviewer high — stayed in the maintainer-side files. A consumer would have read one side of a decision this phase insists is unratified and the maintainer's alone. Both halves now ship, and a guard fails if the cost argument appears without its counter.

**What the author-side pass caught before either reviewer reported:** the ten-rows-versus-nine-phases ambiguity, and a consumer count that had counted the file's own self-description as a citation of itself. **What it did not catch: the number whose *source* was wrong.** That limit is now written into the rule, because it is the difference between the two halves of this round.

## Phase 167 (executed 2026-07-30 — Wave 1 item 5: the test-decision gate that read `main` while gating a branch, plus the folded-in `reset --hard`)

**The defect, and why it fires on every task on every run.** `/review-close` Step 2d — the Phase-59 "verify the record" gate — resolved each claimed task's body as a **plain relative path**. `/claim-task` *decides* the `## Test decision` at plan time, but the **reviewer-executor writes it during implementation, inside the worktree** (`claim-task/SKILL.md` § *Test decision*), so the section is committed on the feature branch and nowhere else. Step 2d runs at Step 2; nothing merges until Step 3b/4a, so `HEAD` is still `main`. The path therefore resolved to `main`'s copy of the body, which for a task claimed this cycle carries **no test-decision heading at all** — every shipped body-author is told not to write one (`intake:111`, `add-task:62`, `onboard:95`). So the gate classified the record `missing` for every task on every code-touching branch on every run, and each `missing` fired its `AskUserQuestion` halt: a gate that only ever reported the state of a revision it was not gating. **Both halves of that sentence were wrong in this phase's first draft and the round caught them.** It said the body held *the schema's template placeholder* — false, that is a template nothing normally copies, and the claim contradicted this phase's own Invariant-13 filing four paragraphs later, which correctly says the section is simply absent. And it said *every task on every run* — false for doc-only branches, which step 0 skips before any record is read. The wrong version had already reached five surfaces (shipped skill prose, this log, the archive, the commit message, the test docstring), which is the cost of writing a mechanism you have not traced to its writer.

**Both specs had it right all along, which is what makes this a drift rather than a design change.** `WORKFLOW.md` § 2.8 says the gate reads "the `## Test decision` section the planner wrote into **each approved branch's task body**", and `WORKFLOW_GUIDE.md` § Merge Process says "read **the branch's** `## Test decision` back against the diff". The skill was the one place that dropped the qualifier — and it is the only place that executes. The fix points Step 2d at `git show <branch>:<body path>`, which is the object-database read Step 2b's own sub-agent prompt already prescribes (`:305`) and the same revision `git diff main...<branch>` reports; both halves of the gate now come from one revision.

**A fourth classification, because the honest failure had nowhere to go.** `git show` can report that the path does not exist at the branch tip — reachable because `claim_task.sh` **reuses** a pre-existing branch rather than refusing (`:486-491`), so a branch cut before the body file was written has no blob. Folding that into `missing` would report a fabricated finding: nothing has been asserted about the record either way. It classifies `unreadable`, halts, and names the revision it read. Step 2d's halt condition and the Step 8 tally both carry it, because a classification no downstream step consumes is invisible — the same gap Step 2b's skip tally closes for conventions.

**The class sweep found one sibling site and one false path gloss.** Step 2a step 3 reads the *same* body, for alignment, by the same plain path — milder (it produces no false halt) but wrong in the same way, since the branch edits its own body. It now reads at the branch tip too. That sentence also carried a **false path**: it glossed the body as `tasks/<status>/<TASK_ID>.md`, and there is **no `tasks/in_progress/` directory anywhere in the tree** (`grep -rn tasks/in_progress core/ docs/ install.sh tests/` → zero hits) — `in_progress` is the status *every* approved branch's task is in, so the gloss was wrong precisely where it was used. A claim never moves the body; the only rename is Step 4c's archive move, which runs after this step. **Four further sites of that gloss are filed rather than fixed** (`document-work:47`, `WORKFLOW.md:112`/`:114`/`:135`) — the sweep is done and recorded in the filing so the next phase does not re-derive it.

**One class member is filed, not fixed, and the reason is design not scope.** `validate_tasks.py` Invariant 13 reads the same record off the filesystem, so run on `main` it warns for the whole `in_progress` window — structurally, not occasionally. Teaching a static per-repo validator about branch state is a design change, and Invariant 13 is warn-only by construction ("a backstop, never a merge gate"), so the noise costs nothing a gate would. Filed with that reasoning attached.

**The folded-in second defect: `git reset --hard origin/main` was ungated tree-wide.** Filed by Phase 165's round, and the brief asked for it to ride with Wave 1 item 4 or 5 rather than open a phase. `review-close:1109` ran it in the **main checkout** at the end of the `pr`-policy close while the surrounding prose explained only *which commits* it discards; it also discards every uncommitted modification to a tracked file there. Nothing gated it: Step 1a's `dirty` classifier **excludes the worktree whose branch is `main`**, Step 1b's porcelain checks do not gate the tree (`:148` is path-scoped to `review_tasks.md`; `:157` is unscoped but only greps its output for a sibling archive file — an earlier draft called both path-scoped, corrected by the round), and `_shared/main-push-guard.md` contains no clean/dirty language at all. It now runs behind `git diff --quiet HEAD --`, with a `DIRTY` arm that refuses, reports `git status --porcelain --untracked-files=no`, and is **forbidden from stashing on the user's behalf** — a stash this skill creates is consumed by no later step, so it would convert a visible refusal into work parked where nobody looks.

**The gate belongs at Step 6, not Step 1, and that is the non-obvious half.** Step 5's staging-deploy wait is a long idle window — exactly when a human is most likely to have edits open — so a Step 1 reading would be stale by the time the reset runs.

**It narrows a promoted convention, and says so.** Both shipped maps name `git reset --hard` explicitly: `convention_map.md` § *Destructive command gating* wants it "preceded by an explicit 'ask the user to confirm' instruction", `security_map.md` § *Confirmation gates on destructive operations* wants "an explicit confirmation step in the skill text". This gate confirms **conditionally** — only when the reset would actually destroy something — because the reset is otherwise either a no-op or a load-bearing re-sync, and an unconditional prompt would land on every close of the dominant `pr` path (this repo's own) while buying nothing in the clean case. Stated in the skill as a deliberate narrowing rather than silently taken, so the next auditor reads a decision instead of a violation.

**Fold-in verdict, stated plainly:** `:1109` is **not** the same step and **not** the same class as item 5 — one is a wrong-revision read, the other a wholesale destructive op. It rode along because it is in the same file, on the same daily path, and small; the two changes are independently reviewable and independently guarded.

**What the author-side pass caught, before any reviewer was spawned.** Three things, and one of them was in the deliverable rather than the guard:

1. **The gate's first draft was the over-refusal bug the fix exists to avoid.** It tested `git status --porcelain`, which includes untracked files — but `git reset --hard` leaves untracked files alone, and an untracked scratch file is ordinary in a live repo (this repo carries one). That gate would have refused **every** close. Rewritten to `git diff --quiet HEAD --`. This is § *Before you spawn anyone* rule 1's "over-strictness, the direction that hides" finding its own author, and mutation 7 in the committed table now pins it.
2. **Two false claims in prose written minutes earlier** (rule 2): the note cited `WORKFLOW.md § 3` for a line that is in **§ 2.8**, and it attributed the verbatim quote *"an explicit confirmation step in the skill text"* to **both** maps when it is `security_map.md`'s wording alone. Both corrected before commit.
3. **The guard's population was derived from the file under test rather than the source of truth.** Step 2d's new note *cites* `WORKFLOW.md` and `WORKFLOW_GUIDE.md` as the specs it aligns to — so a drift there would make the shipped note false while every skill-scoped assertion stayed green. Added `check_the_cited_spec_still_says_what_is_cited`, plus a direct non-vacuity test for it, because the mutation table only edits the skill and cannot reach it.

**The round: three reviewers, distinct lenses, one on a different model — and it disqualified the first version of both halves.** Lenses: *does it execute* / *are its claims true* / *are its tests real*. The count was a judgement call (filed as the maintainer's open decision); three lenses were chosen over more reviewers on the same lens because Phase 166 measured ~15% overlap with each lens producing its sharpest finding alone. That held again: **no finding below was reached by two lenses.**

**Two defects in the shipped fix, both from the execute lens, both of which would have replaced one always-halt with another.**

1. **The prescribed command could not read the canonical `body:` path.** The note asserted "a `git show <rev>:<path>` path is repo-root-relative, **which is the form `body:` already records**." `tasks/schema.md` § body says the opposite in bold: *"**Canonical shape:** `open/<TASK-ID>.md` — relative to `tasks/`, without the `tasks/` prefix … **NOT** `tasks/open/FEAT-0001.md`."* Three shipped readers implement a two-branch resolver for exactly this (`validate_tasks.py:441-447`, `next_task.py`, `scope_overlap.py`), and every shipped writer emits the canonical form (`intake:113`/`:138`, `add-task:62`, `document-work:199`), so on a fresh install **100% of live `body:` values** take the branch the fix ignored. Executed: `git show feat/FEAT-0001:open/FEAT-0001.md` → `fatal: path … does not exist`. That fatal is the exact signature of this phase's own new `unreadable` arm — so the fix would have halted every close **with a fabricated diagnosis blaming the branch**, which is the failure the `unreadable` bullet was written to prevent. The skill contradicted itself 492 lines later, where `:838` already calls `open/<TASK_ID>.md` canonical. Now resolved with the shipped two-branch rule, and `unreadable` opens by telling the reader to re-check the prefix first, because a mis-resolved path is the likelier cause.
2. **The fenced command was a syntax error as written.** `git show <branch>:<body path>` — unquoted `<…>` is a bash redirection, not a placeholder, and the operand contains a space. Verified: `bash: syntax error near unexpected token 'newline'`. **This same file states that exact rule at `:1139`** for `git branch -D`, added by an earlier phase. Now quoted; an unquoted path containing a space also truncated silently into the `unreadable` bucket.

**One defect in the fix from the tests lens: a classification tallied in one place and dropped from the report a human reads.** Step 8's template (`:1224`) still read `<N verified, N waived, N held-for-fix, N doc-only>`. The commit message claimed `unreadable` was "carried into the halt condition and the Step 8 tally" — true of Step 2d's internal tally line, false of Step 8, and the check that claimed to cover "Step 8's tally" was reading Step 2d. Fixed at the template and pinned there.

**Three false claims in the record, from the claims lens.** Two are corrected in place above (the placeholder mechanism; the unqualified "every task every run"). The third is bookkeeping and it matters more than it looks: the archive section asserted this item *"never had a `REVIEW_CHECKLIST.md` entry of its own"* — false. **Leg (e) of the Phase-164 residue entry names `review-close:338` explicitly**, and it was left reading as open work in the active queue while the archive declared it resolved. Phase 165 had set the correct precedent by striking its sibling leg inline. Struck now. Also corrected: a filed grep recipe stated as returning "zero hits" in the present tense, which is true of the parent commit and **false in the tree that ships the sentence** (this phase's own prose adds the hits) — now version-anchored; and a "both specs already said the branch's record" claim that overstated `WORKFLOW.md` § 2.8, which scopes *whose* body rather than *which revision*. `WORKFLOW_GUIDE.md` is the one that genuinely specifies the revision, so it is now cited as the spec restored and § 2.8 as merely consistent.

**And the guard module was disqualified outright.** A reviewer ran **90 mutations and 43 were genuine bypasses.** The defect was uniform and is the failure mode this project keeps re-learning: eight of the nine checks asserted a *token* appeared in a line, and a line here is routinely a 700-character paragraph, so "N phrases in a sentence asserting the opposite" walked through every one. Three demonstrated survivors, each of which ships the defect the phase exists to remove:

- **The read instruction inverted.** `Read the body from the working tree … Do **not** read it **at the branch tip** … and ignore the older instruction that said "never the working-tree copy"` — all three required tokens present, meaning reversed. This is verbatim the failure `test_review_close_diff_basis.py`'s docstring records from Phase 158, reproduced one file over by an author who had read it.
- **The gate arms swapped.** `git diff --quiet HEAD -- && echo "DIRTY …" || echo "CLEAN — safe to reset"`. `git diff --quiet` exits **0 when clean**, so this fires `reset --hard` **exactly when it destroys work**. The author's table applied directional inversion to `unreadable` and never to the gate — the one place where inversion is data loss.
- **The gate commented out.** `gate_at` was a bare `find`, while the *reset* side of the same check carefully restricted itself to executable lines. The asymmetry made "the gate comes first" satisfiable by any prose mention.

Three further structural defects: **`_slice`'s docstring was false** — with the end marker absent it returned the rest of the file, silently widening the Step 2d window from 7,890 to 96,821 characters, so a renamed downstream heading let content from anywhere satisfy a 2d assertion; the over-strictness scan for untracked-inclusive `git status --porcelain` **excluded the one prose site it was written about**; and **15 innocent edits went red** — rewrapping, a `-`→`*` bullet, `halt and ask`→`halt and prompt` (which `WORKFLOW.md:341`, the cited spec, already says) — the brittleness that trains people to weaken guards.

**So the primitive changed.** Load-bearing sentences are now **pinned verbatim, whitespace-normalised**: 27 pins across four sections, plus an 8-entry contradiction screen for the reversals that could survive by quoting a pin inside a negation, executable-line discipline on **both** sides of the ordering check with the gate line pinned including its arm direction, a `_slice` that fails closed, and a spec-population check that resolves `WORKFLOW.md`'s § number rather than trusting it. Rewrapping and reflowing now pass; changing the words does not.

**Guards: 6 checks over 27 pins, a committed 25-mutation table, and a pre-fix regression probe.** `tests/test_review_close_record_revision.py` holds pure functions of the skill text (with one deliberate exception, the spec-population check, whose docstring says so — the module-level "every check is a pure function" claim was itself false in the first version and the round caught it). `MUTATIONS` now carries **the round's demonstrated bypasses as permanent regression tests**, not the author's self-selected set: 25 entries, every one of which passed all nine of the old checks or names a defect the round found in the fix itself. **All 27 pins are absent from the pre-fix text**, which is the honest form of the old "8 of 9 checks red" number — check *count* stopped being meaningful once eight token checks collapsed into one pin check.

**A post-rewrite battery of 28 mutations that are deliberately not in the committed table** — including twelve of the reviewer's survivors the table does not pin, plus new shapes (a `--cached`-only gate, a backslash-continued gate, a second ungated reset added later, a swapped canonical/back-compat comment) — ran **24/24 real regressions caught and 4/4 innocent reformats green**. It found one more hole in the rewrite, now closed: the ordering check compared first-gate to first-reset, so **a second executable reset added later was ungated**; Step 6 now asserts exactly one of each. Reporting this separately from the committed table is the point — a table you wrote cannot measure your own blind spot, which is what the § *Before you spawn anyone* rule exists to say. Suite: **1874 → 1909 passed, 4 skipped** (verified by a full run, not by adding up the new tests — an earlier draft said 1895 from arithmetic and the round's independent full runs confirmed 1874 at the parent).

## Phase 168 (executed 2026-07-30 — the third author-side-pass rule: run the commands the change prescribes)

**The filing's own evidence, re-executed rather than restated.** `_shared/adversarial-review.md` named this defect class as the author-side pass's blind spot and did nothing about it: *"a prescribed command that fails on the operator's own machine."* Phase 167 then shipped one. The rule that closes it has two halves, and the second is the one that does the work — a fixture built from the author's model tests only that the author is self-consistent. That claim is the phase's central assertion, so it was executed first, before any prose was written, in a throwaway `git init` repo whose `body:` value came from the shipped writers rather than from memory: `git show "feat/FEAT-0001:tasks/open/FEAT-0001.md"` printed the file and **exited 0**; `git show "feat/FEAT-0001:open/FEAT-0001.md"` — the canonical shape `tasks/schema.md` § `body` requires and `intake/SKILL.md` emits — **exited 128** with `fatal: path 'open/FEAT-0001.md' does not exist in 'feat/FEAT-0001'`. Same fixture, same resolver, opposite verdicts. The rule is dogfooded by construction: its only concrete operand is that command, and running it is what licensed the sentence.

**The precondition was the whole reason the filing had its shape, and it is a real one.** Rules 1 and 2 sat at `:55` and `:66`; `:68` was the *"What this pass cannot do"* paragraph, whose first sentence read *"It never executes the change against real state"* and whose first example was the exact defect rule 3 now catches. A rule 3 inserted between them falsifies the paragraph that follows them. `:68` is therefore rewritten in the same edit — **scoped, not deleted**: executing one command against a fixture *you* built reaches "does it run" and "does it do what I said" and stops there, and what stays out of reach is whether the prescribed command is the *right* one, whether a claim about what its output *means* holds, the common case itself (a fixture is one case and the author chose which), and a number whose *source* was wrong. Shipping the rule with `:68` intact would have been a self-contradicting partial in the file that exists to prevent them.

**The honest limit ships inside the rule, not only in the paragraph below it.** Rule 3 reaches whether the command runs and whether it does what its author said. In Phase 167's round the other two defect classes — 43 of 90 guard mutations bypassing, three false claims in the record — were entirely outside it. It converts one expensive finding into a cheap one; it does not replace a lens. That clause is pinned, because deleting it turns the rule into an argument for fewer reviewers, which the § *Decisions to revisit later* record says is the maintainer's call and which Phase 166's ~15% measured overlap argues against.

**A filed number that did not survive checking.** The filing says the partial is consumed by **8 skills**, naming `intake` and `test-audit`. `grep -rln "adversarial-review.md" core/skills/` returns **6 skills** (`auto-build`, `claim-task`, `codebase-review`, `plan-review`, `review-close`, `security-audit`) **and 3 `_shared/` partials** (`fanout-evidence`, `guided-mode`, `test-assessment-rubric`). `intake` mentions "the adversarial-review rubric" as an analogy for the decomposition rubric and `test-audit` cites "adversarial-review #7" as a dimension; neither reads the file. The blast radius is 9 consumers, not 11, and it still ships to consumers in both install modes.

**What the author-side pass caught, before any reviewer was spawned** — reported separately from the round below, per the rule this phase is adding to.

1. **Two vacuity holes in the phase's own new guards.** The innocent-reformat twin applied three `str.replace` calls and never asserted any of them changed the text — a reformat that silently no-ops passes while proving nothing, which is the vacuity class this module is named for, reached through its own negative control. Fixed with a no-op assertion per reformat. Second, the subsection slicer was the fail-open shape Phase 167's round measured one file over: on a missing end marker it returned the rest of the file, so the Prompt Template's nine review dimensions could stand in for a rule of this subsection. Now fails closed on a named end marker, with its own test.
2. **A generalisation that silently dropped a class, caught by the phase's own mutation table.** Replacing the five literal forbidden phrases with class patterns lost coverage of `"optional for prose-only changes"` — a change-class carve-out, and docs-only is precisely where an unchallenged claim ships. The committed table went red on the mutation that had been passing five minutes earlier. Restored as a pattern rather than the literal.
3. **An over-strict pre-existing guard, in the direction rule 1 calls "the direction that hides."** The `_HEDGES` entry `usually enough` — written about reviewer *count* — reddened the innocent sentence *"a scratch `git init` is usually enough of a fixture."* Narrowed to require a reviewer-ish subject; the softened-section fixture still trips it. A guard that reddens on innocent prose is what trains people to weaken guards, which is the Phase-167 finding this repo paid 15 innocent reds to learn.

**Guards: the pin primitive, and six author-side batteries that disagreed with it.** `tests/test_adversarial_review_gate.py` is extended, not replaced — the existing token-presence predicates keep guarding rules 1 and 2, where Phase 166's round validated them. Rule 3 gets `test_review_close_record_revision.py`'s primitive: **19 verbatim whitespace-normalised pins** resolved against the rule-3 block (not the subsection — see the round), a regex contradiction screen, a permissive-modal screen, fail-closed slicers on both the subsection and the block, a placement check that resolves rule 2 / rule 3 / the limits paragraph from unique verbatim anchors, and a both-halves conditional.

**The batteries are the measurement, and they are reported because they kept losing.** Six batteries, none written into the committed table at the time it ran: **16/20 · 5/12 · 5/12 · 6/12 · 4/14 · 11/12.** Every survivor across the first five was the same class — **addition**. A contradicting sentence added *beside* an intact pin leaves every pin intact by construction, and enumeration lost the race outright: each new battery produced a fresh family (supersession, redefinition of "source of truth", `<details>` collapse, an appended *"Or after, if that is more convenient"* carrying no modal at all). The fifth scored *worse* than the second against a screen that had grown twice.

**So the answer was structural.** Commented-out, fenced, blockquoted and `<details>`-collapsed prose is stripped before slicing — in this file `>` marks prompt text, so blockquoting does not soften a rule, it re-addresses it to the reviewer whose cost the rule exists to lower. The subsection heading must occur **exactly once** or the slicer fails closed, because a softened decoy planted anywhere above steals `find`'s window while the real rule sits outside it untouched. And the block's free space is **pinned rather than budgeted** — see the round, which killed the character ratchet that first occupied that slot.

**The committed table is 52 mutations, and it is not the author's own set.** M1–M18 are the shapes written alongside the guards. **M19–M52 are 34 entries drawn from the batteries and the round: 33 are demonstrated survivors** — battery 5's ten are represented by its four families rather than all ten, to keep the table readable — **plus one caught shape (M30) kept for coverage.** Reporting the two groups apart is the point: a table you wrote cannot measure your own blind spot, which is the § *Before you spawn anyone* claim this phase is extending.

## Phase 168's adversarial round

**Three reviewers, distinct lenses, fresh context, worktree-isolated, read-only** — *does it execute* / *are its claims true* / *are its tests real*. Three was the count, matching Phase 167's calibration and Phase 166's ~15% measured overlap. The tree was verified clean and at the phase commit afterwards. **No finding below was reached by two lenses.**

**The claims lens found a false claim in the shipped rule text — the class this phase exists to remove, in the phase that adds the rule.** Rule 3 asserted that a command in a skill's fenced block *"is read as `text` by every mechanism that guards it."* Four modules falsify it: `test_review_close_smoke_gate.py`, `test_review_close_close_heredoc.py`, `test_batch_claim_kinds.py` and `test_round_markers.py` each extract a **named** heredoc from a skill file and execute it against a fixture repo. The author-side pass did not catch it because the pass re-read the new prose against the *rule's* sources and never against the test tree. The surviving claim is **no *general* runner**, not *no runner*, and that is what now ships — with the four modules named in the pin's rationale so the next author meets the counter-evidence before rewriting the sentence.

**Two more claims corrected in shipped prose.** *"One reviewer found it, and in one way only: by building a scratch repo and running the string"* overstates its own source: Phase 167's record grounds that finding in **reading** as well — `tasks/schema.md` § body *"says the opposite in bold"*, three shipped resolvers, every shipped writer, and a self-contradiction 492 lines later in the same skill — with execution as corroboration. It now says one of three lenses found it and the other two read the same files and did not, which is the part the record actually supports. And *"three false claims in the record"* inherits a number its source contradicts: Phase 167's section is **headed** three and its body corrects **five**. The count is dropped rather than picked, and the pin's rationale says why.

**Three numbers in this phase's own record were wrong, and the arithmetic one is the worst.** *"The fourth battery scored worse than the second"* — 6/12 against 5/12; the fourth scored **better**. The fifth (4/14) is the one that scored worse. The pin count said 17 against a list of **20 entries, 19 distinct** — with one byte-identical duplicate, now removed. And the assertion message said *"27 softenings"* where the first five batteries produced **34**.

**The execute lens killed the growth ratchet, which was the phase's answer to the whole addition class.** It shipped with 30 characters of slack, and `Skip it if rushed.` is 19: **74 passed**. Worse, a ceiling bounds the block's *size* while the free space is size minus pins — so deleting 110 characters of unpinned prose (*"Those want a reader who has not already decided what the change means…"*) buys a 139-character softening asserting that *"a careful read of the command discharges this step just as well … and the fixture is then redundant"* — the exact belief rule 3 refutes — at a net length that fits: **74 passed**. Both verified by me before acting. The author's table could never have found this: all three of its addition entries add 38+ characters, so it only ever demonstrated the guard firing *above* the slack, and the ratchet's own control permitted a slack twice the size of the sentences that walked through it.

**So the residue is pinned instead of budgeted.** `RULE_3_BLOCK_VERBATIM` is the whole rule-3-plus-limits block, verbatim, normalised for whitespace **and** list markers (`*` and `1.` fold to `-` while line starts are still visible — folding after flattening would mistake *"exited 128. This is rule 1's…"* for an ordered marker). Any edit to the block — added, deleted, swapped or relocated sentence — fails until the constant is updated in the same commit, which puts the rule change and its re-approval in one diff, and the message names the first divergence. The character ratchet is gone.

**The same lens found the pins were matched against the wrong window.** They resolved against the whole subsection, so a pinned sentence could be **moved out of rule 3 into rule 2** and still satisfy its own pin; CI went red only as a knock-on, naming an unrelated mutation. Pins now resolve against the block. The contradiction screens stay section-wide on purpose — a contradiction planted *beside* the rule still contradicts it.

**The tests lens ran its own battery — 51 mutations, 24 survivors — and two of its families were still open after the fixes above.** It ran against the phase commit, so the ratchet defeats it reported (length-neutral shrink-and-add, sub-slack softenings, factual inversions in unpinned prose) were already closed by the verbatim pin by the time I re-verified; I checked each rather than assuming. Two were not:

- **The subsection ABOVE rule 3 was ungoverned — 8 of 8 survived.** The modal screen and the verbatim pin were scoped to rule 3 and its limits paragraph, so a sentence in the *preamble* saw only the pins. Four I re-verified myself, all green: *"Rule 3 does not bind a docs-only change."* · *"Throughout this subsection, `source of truth` means the author's best current understanding of the shipped behaviour."* · *"The order of the three rules carries no requirement."* (which retires the before-you-spawn precondition this phase exists for) · *"Where the literal string is awkward to run, a close paraphrase of it is fine."* None touches rule 3. All four govern how it reads. **So the pin's window is the whole subsection**, and the four are pinned as M49–M52.
- **A contradiction planted *above* the `###` heading is outside every subsection-scoped guard.** `Docs-only phases are exempt from the author-side pass below.` — `are exempt` was already in `_BLANKET_EXEMPTIONS`, but that list ran only inside the subsection, and `section_problems` applied only `_HEDGES`. Both screens now run over the whole `## Running more than one reviewer` section. A sibling, *"Rule 3 of the author-side pass below is advisory"*, then showed the demotion pattern was adjacency-anchored (`rule 3 is advisory`) and walked past it; it is subject-anchored now.

**Two vacuity findings from the same lens, both real.** Deleting `rule_3_placement_problems` from `RULE_3_CHECKS` left the module green — every table entry that reorders the rules also breaks the verbatim pin, so the table could never isolate it. And `_rule_3_block`'s fail-closed branch was a docstring claim with no guard: replacing it with `pass` left 74 tests passing. Both now have direct tests, which is what the module already demanded of its own spec-population check one file over.

**Post-round measurement, both numbers.** Re-run against the hardened guards, the six author-side batteries catch **82 of 82** regressions, and every family the tests lens demonstrated is caught. Of the batteries' 30 innocent edits, **11 stay green and 19 now go red.** The split is clean and it is the cost of the primitive: every red is a *content* edit inside the subsection — adding a sentence, rewording an unpinned clause, an emphasis or punctuation change — while every pure-formatting edit passes, confirmed by re-indenting, swapping bullet markers, folding ordered lists, splitting a hyphenated word across lines, and reflowing the whole subsection to 70 and 80 columns.

**Read that as a cost, not a win.** The subsection's wording is now frozen: changing it means regenerating a 7.6 KB constant in the same commit, and the failure message carries the one-line recipe. The justification is narrow and should stay narrow — five author-side batteries and a reviewer's 51-mutation battery both showed that every *scoped* guard loses to addition, and this is the only thing that closed it. It is right for one contested subsection that ships to consumers. It would be wrong for a file.

**The round's own fixes exposed brittleness in the harness, which is the direction that hides.** Verifying against innocent reformats turned the suite red six ways, none of them a defect in the document: `_sub`'s anchors are raw file text while the checks they feed are whitespace-normalised, so rewrapping a pinned sentence produced `mutation source text not found`; six structural mutations sliced by `t.index()` and raised a bare `ValueError` when a `-` bullet became `*`; two anchors pinned the list marker itself, which Phase 167 had already recorded as a mistake one file over; `author_pass_problems` matched Phase 166's patterns against raw text, so reflowing the limits paragraph split *"cannot catch a number whose `source` was wrong"* across a newline and the guard reported the rule **gone**; hard-wrapping at 80 columns split `purpose-built` and `plan-review` and did the same; and `test_innocent_reformats_stay_green`'s own probes were fixed substitutions that no-op'd once the file already carried that formatting, so applying the very reformat the test blesses failed it. All six closed: tolerant anchors, a tolerant offset helper, markers dropped from anchors, flattened matching, a hyphen-break fold, and toggles instead of substitutions.

**A filed number that did not survive checking.** The filing says the partial is consumed by **8 skills**, naming `intake` and `test-audit`. `grep -rln "adversarial-review.md" core/skills/` returns **6 skills** (`auto-build`, `claim-task`, `codebase-review`, `plan-review`, `review-close`, `security-audit`) **and 3 `_shared/` partials** (`fanout-evidence`, `guided-mode`, `test-assessment-rubric`); `intake` mentions "the adversarial-review rubric" as an analogy and `test-audit` cites "adversarial-review #7" as a dimension, and neither reads the file. Independently confirmed by the claims lens. The blast radius is 9 consumers, not 11, and it still ships in both install modes.

**One thing the round checked and cleared:** the rule's two headline verdicts. The execute lens rebuilt the fixture from the source of truth and got `exit 0` on `tasks/open/FEAT-0001.md` and `exit 128` — `fatal: path … does not exist` — on the canonical `open/FEAT-0001.md`, matching the sentence the phase ships. `install.sh --help` and `--mode loop` both exit 0 with the partial installed and rule 3 intact.

## Phase 169 (executed 2026-07-30 — Wave 1 item 2: the phantom shell variables, and the sentence that licensed six more of them)

**The filed item was 20 sites in 2 files. The class was 33 in 5, and the thirteen extra were the ones a previous sweep had looked at and cleared — or could not see.**

Ground rule: a skill is markdown an agent executes, and nothing carries from one fenced block to the next. A `$VAR` its own block does not assign is the empty string when the command runs. Phase 164 filed 20 such sites — `/auto-build` 18, `/claim-task` 2 — as Wave 1 item 2.

**Two consequences were live, and both were silent.** `git -C "" rev-parse HEAD` does not fail; it runs in the CWD and prints a real SHA (verified in a scratch repo). So `/auto-build`'s Phase-6a integrity check, **run as written**, compared that against an empty `$PRE_PLAN_HEAD`, was always true, and parked **every task in the batch** while reporting a plan-only contract violation that had not happened. The round pushed back on "every run" and was right to: the pre-fix prose two paragraphs below the block did say the value is held in context, so an orchestrator that substituted anyway would have been fine, and there are no run logs either way. The mechanism is measured; the frequency is not, and is no longer claimed. And an empty `"$SUBSET_IDS"` made `/auto-build TECH-A TECH-B` select from the whole open frontier — the exact inversion of the "requested IDs are never silently dropped" invariant Step 1 states two paragraphs above the bug.

### The class sweep, which is where the phase actually went

The brief's first standing instruction is *do not fix a finding without sweeping its class*, and its second is *do not adopt a shipped skill's justification clause as authority* — filed because Phase 164 broke both while running the phase built to enforce them. It had excluded eight of its 28 raw hits by citing two warrants. **Both warrants were false, and the exclusions with them.**

- **`/review-close`'s `$APPROVED_BRANCH`×6 — a real defect, excused by a note whose own scope claim was wrong.** The note said the value is "referenced in Steps 4a–4d" and told the reader to re-export "at the top of each later `pr`-policy step". Verified: `APPROVED_BRANCH` is assigned once, at `:657`, and every one of its six reads is in Step 4-**pre** — `grep` finds **zero** references at or after Step 4a. So the remedy prescribed re-exports for steps that never read it and nothing for the step that did. It also sat 44–59 lines *after* the blocks it was cited to govern, while two comments *inside* those blocks taught the opposite model.
- **What that cost, measured rather than asserted.** With the name empty: `git fetch origin ""` **exits 0** and prints a normal-looking `* branch HEAD -> FETCH_HEAD` without refreshing any remote-tracking ref — falsifying the comment that used to sit on that line; `git rev-list --count "..origin/"` fatals and prints nothing; `git rev-list --count "..origin/main"` **prints a plausible number**, silently answering `HEAD..origin/main`. Because condition 4 printed nothing, the skill's own rule read that as "conditions unmet" and fell through. **So the entire PR-reuse shape — a Phase-151 feature — has been unreachable on every run since it shipped, fail-safe and therefore invisible.** Fixing the phantoms makes it reachable again, which is a real behaviour change and is called out as one.
- **Three more sites no fenced-block sweep can see.** `/review-close` Step 4a's merge commands are numbered-list items in backticks, not a fenced block, and all three read a `$MERGE_TARGET` set one step earlier. The maintainer sweeper reported a clean 9 pairs while they sat in the file. Inline code has no block to be assigned in, so a `$VAR` in one is cross-block by construction.
- **`main-push-guard`'s `$EXPECTED_BRANCH`×2 — correctly excluded, on a ground that is not in the file.** It is fail-closed (an empty expected branch makes the assert always STOP) and no consumer copies it: four inline the literal `main` (`/claim-task`, `/auto-build`, `/release`, and `/document-work` in its inverted `!= "main"` form) and `/review-close` asserts a fixed `merge/review-close-*` pattern, verified by grep. But nothing in the file *declares* it a template; the only supporting text is a comment defining what the value means, and it is written in variable syntax where the repo's idiom is `<angle brackets>`, which is exactly what makes a placeholder indistinguishable from a runnable reference. Converted rather than re-excluded, so it leaves every future sweep for good.

### The root cause, which is upstream of all 33

`WORKFLOW.md` § 8.2a stated the rule at **step** granularity — *"skill steps are separate shell calls"* — and that is where `/review-close`'s note, `/claim-task`'s Step 2 rule, `permission-guard.md` and the maintainer sweeper's own docstring all got it. A step is a `##` heading: prose, with no mechanical realization. Nothing binds the blocks under one heading into a single shell call. **Under a step-granular reading the six `/review-close` sites are fine, which is precisely why they shipped and why a sweep cleared them.**

§ 8.2a now states the boundary as the block, and states it deliberately as a **requirement on the author rather than a claim about the runner** — "assume nothing survives from one fenced block to the next" holds however the harness batches, where "each block is a separate call" would itself be an unverified mechanism assertion, the defect class this repo keeps shipping. This is the Phase-165 shape one file over: a fix confined to the skills leaves the row that licenses the belief.

### What shipped

33 sites converted across `/auto-build` (18), `/claim-task` (2), `/review-close` (9 — six fenced, three inline), `main-push-guard` (2), `/daily-summary` (2, found by the round); four now-unreachable `MERGE_TARGET=`/`APPROVED_BRANCH=` assignments dropped with them; § 8.2a's rule corrected, along with **six** restatements of it — three the phase found (`permission-guard.md`, `/claim-task` Step 2, `/review-close`'s note) and three its round did (`/auto-build`, `/security-audit`, and the maintainer worklist's own docstring, which this phase had edited 25 lines below the stale line without noticing it). Two structural fixes rode along because the phantoms hid them: `/auto-build` Phase 6a *instructed* a pre-plan HEAD capture without ever giving the command, in a paragraph printed **after** the block that consumed it (now a hoisted bare `git … rev-parse HEAD` read before the spawn), and Phase 6e's capture was an assignment whose value could not reach its Phase-7 reader.

**The gate is `tests/test_phantom_shell_vars.py`** — two zero-invariants (fenced blocks, inline commands) over every skill, six non-vacuity twins that all call the production predicate so neutering it reddens its own twin, verbatim whitespace-normalised pins on § 8.2a's rule and on the retired step wording, and per-site pins. The maintainer sweeper is demoted to a worklist and now records its three limits, one of which was a live hole: **`REPO_ROOT` sat in its exempt set and nothing in the tree exports it** — it is script-local to `claim_task.sh`, `batch_work.sh` and the merge hook, where variables persist normally. The exempt set is pinned, because adding a name to it is the cheapest way to silence the guard.

**Author-side pass (rule 3 — run the commands the change prescribes).** Ran, and it is what found the two `git` behaviours above; the empty-operand results are measured, not reasoned. It also caught the phase breaking `test_heredoc_permission_idiom`'s opener regex, which had pinned `"$VAR"` as the *only* legal positional arg — so converting the four heredocs to literals dropped its corpus from 7 to 3 and its own floor caught it. **That regex was ratcheting the defect in place**, as were four probe strings in `test_review_close_pr_policy`; both were widened, with the shape question left where it was and the content question moved to the new module.

**Mutation-verified: 35 of 35.** Each fix reverted individually, guards re-run, tree restored. The first draft killed 34 — the survivor was inverting `/claim-task` Step 2's *"Do not carry it in a shell variable"* to *"You may"*. The code guards would catch the next `$TASK_ID`; nothing caught the sentence inviting it, which is the same licence-vs-call-site split as the § 8.2a root cause, one file down. Pinned.

**Rule 2 of the pass — re-read your own new prose against the code it describes — caught two errors in this record before the round saw it, and one of them was the headline number.** (The round then found four more of the same kind, so rule 2's yield here was real but partial — it catches what you can see by re-reading, not what you have to re-derive.) Every surface said the class was **28**: that is the fenced-block total, and it silently dropped the three inline sites this phase went out of its way to find. The real count is **31**, and the wrong one had already propagated to six places (this entry, `CLAUDE.md`'s row, the checklist, the archive, the brief, the commit message) — the same one-retraction-never-propagates failure this phase is fixing in Phase 164's record, reproduced inside the phase fixing it. The second: "all five consumers inline their own literal" was false for `/review-close`, which asserts a pattern rather than a literal. Both corrected. **Note what rule 2 did *not* catch and no author-side rule can:** whether 31 is now right depends on the inline detector's command-word list being the right one, which is a judgement a reader who has not already decided what the change means has to make.

**Suite: 1971 → 1990 passed + 4 skipped.**

## Phase 169's adversarial round

Three fresh-context `general-purpose` reviewers, worktree-isolated, read-only, on distinct lenses — **does it execute** / **are its claims true** / **are the guards real**. Reviewer count was my judgement call (the count is still filed as Wade's under § Decisions): three, because the change touches five shipped skills plus the spec, and because its own author-side pass had already found a wrong headline number, which is evidence the prose layer needed more than one reader. Every finding below I re-ran myself before acting.

**The round's headline: the mechanical core survived intact and the prose layer did not.** Both lenses that checked it re-derived the site inventory independently and matched — 28 fenced, the same four files, the six `/review-close` reads all inside Step 4-pre, the "since Phase 151" provenance via `git log -S`, and all four measured git behaviours. The claims lens ran its own 17-mutation battery against the guards and killed 17/17. What did not survive was almost entirely sentences I had written this phase.

**One regression the phase introduced, and it was mine, not inherited.** `mkdir -p "<worktree path>/…"` is the single command among all 33 converted sites that does **not** fail on an unsubstituted placeholder: it creates a directory literally named `<worktree path>`, returns 0, and the Phase-6d **park verdict** — the only durable record of why a task parked — lands there while the run reports PARKED. The pre-fix `$WORKTREE_PATH` form failed at filesystem root, so this is strictly a loss the conversion caused. Both sites are now `&&`-gated on a read-only `git -C … rev-parse --show-toplevel`, verified to exit 128 and create nothing. **The general lesson is narrower than "quote it": the quoted-placeholder idiom's fail-loud property is a property of the *command*, not of the idiom**, and it has to be checked per command rather than assumed once.

**One live hazard on a path the phase itself made live, which is the riskiest thing here.** Restoring the PR-reuse shape from unreachable to reachable exposed a defect in its guard: the step claimed a failed `git fetch` makes condition 4 print nothing, so a broken probe falls through safely. Measured false. `refs/remotes/origin/<branch>` survives a failed fetch for any branch that has ever been fetched or pushed — every branch with an open PR, i.e. every branch that can reach the probe — so both counts resolve against **stale** refs and print `0`, which is exactly the answer that takes the reuse shape. With `gh` up over HTTPS and git transport down (expired SSH key — not an exotic state), a branch 1 behind its remote and 1 behind `origin/main` printed `0`/`0`. The step now echoes the fetch's exit status and refuses to read the counts unless it is `0`. **A dormant feature made live is a feature shipped for the first time, and it deserves the scrutiny of one — the phase had treated it as a side effect.**

**Four false or overstated claims in the phase's own new prose, three of them in shipped files.**

- **`/auto-build` Step 5's comment asserted a consequence that does not happen** — that a phantom `"$TASK_ID"` leaves 5.4 committing `claim: mark  as in-progress`, "a real commit on `main` naming no task". Run: 5.1 exits 1 *before* writing `index.yml`, so 5.4 stages nothing and `git commit` fails with `nothing to commit`. No commit. **This is rule 3's own failure mode:** the pass ran the commands whose *operands* the change substituted and never ran the sequence whose *consequence* the change asserted. The rule says "scope this to commands whose operand the change computes or substitutes" — that scoping is what let a fabricated consequence through, and the honest reading is that a claim about what a command *does downstream* needs the same fixture as a claim about whether it runs. The comment now states what the block actually does: there is no `set -e`, so 5.3 and 5.4 run anyway against a tree nothing claimed.
- **The § 8.2a root-cause paragraph shipped an invalid causal chain**, citing the two commands that *hid* the failure (`git fetch origin ""` exiting 0, condition 5 printing a number) as the reason the reuse shape was unreachable, and adding "without ever emitting an error" — false, since condition 4 fatals every time. The one fact that entails unreachability, the condition-4 fatal, was absent. Rewritten. The `PHASE_LOG` version had it right, so the *shipped* surface was the degraded one — the opposite of the direction that gets caught.
- **"Both halves were wrong"** about the retired persistence note was a compound claim rejected wholesale — the scope claim held for two of its three variables. Decomposed, which is the rule Phase 140 shipped and this sentence broke.
- **A `REPO_ROOT` enumeration presented as exhaustive** listed 3 of 9+ assignment sites, in four places. The load-bearing half — nothing *exports* it — is true and independently confirmed.

**The class sweep was incomplete in both directions, and the round found both.** Two more shipped restatements of the retired step-granular rule (`/auto-build`, `/security-audit`) plus the worklist docstring, none visible to a guard keyed to one literal phrasing; and **a fifth file**, `/daily-summary`, calling its own shell functions from inline code outside the block that defines them, where neither the functions nor the `$TARGET_DATE` exist. The inline detector missed it because its command-word list was hardcoded to `git|gh|bash|python3|sh` — so the detector now **derives** each file's shell-function names from its own definitions, which is rule 1's "derive the population from the source of truth" applied to the detector rather than to the files. 31 → 33.

**One finding the round got right, one the phase got wrong in responding to it, and the suite is what settled it.** The execute lens flagged that this phase's new comments say "quoted, so an unsubstituted placeholder fails loudly" while `/claim-task` and `/review-close` write `<TASK_ID>` and `<branch>` bare — a real coherence defect. I quoted three sites, and **four tests went red**: `test_batch_claim_kinds.py::TestEntryStateProseGuards` pins the *unquoted* form on purpose, and its docstring records that an earlier draft pinned the `$TASK_ID` form and reddened the suite when the correct placeholder was written. The unquoted `<PLACEHOLDER>` operand is the house convention — **69 sites** — not a 69-site defect class, which is what I had just filed it as. Reverted, and the filing rewritten to the narrow thing that is actually wrong: `review-close:1071`'s description of the failure mode, which is position-dependent in a way the sentence does not capture. **The generalisable point is that § 8.2a's "write the value out, quoted" is scoped to values that can carry spaces or shell metacharacters and never says so**, which is how a reviewer and an author both read it as universal. That scoping is the filed work. It is also the second time this phase mistook a deliberate convention for a defect — the first was `main-push-guard`, where the exclusion was right and only its stated warrant was wrong — and both times the tell was the same: no shipped sentence said why.

**The tests lens was the expensive one and the one worth the money: 103 mutations, 52 survivors — a 50.5% bypass rate against the guards as committed.** My own battery had reported 35/35 on the same commit. Both numbers are true and they measure different things, which is the lesson: **every one of my 35 was "revert the exact edit I just made at the site I just changed."** Not one planted a *new* phantom, probed a detector boundary, probed the file population, or deleted a test. A revert battery measures that the guard is wired to the file; it says nothing about coverage — which is precisely the failure `_shared/adversarial-review.md` § *the author-side pass* rule 1 describes, written by Phase 166, and I reproduced it while following the rule.

**Its headline was a live site my own gate could not see, and the gate was strictly weaker than the tool it replaced.** `fenced_blocks` blanked any fenced line starting with `>` as a blockquoted illustration. A shell redirection continued onto its own line —

```
echo "PLAN_PHASE_VIOLATION: …" \
  > "$WORKTREE_PATH/…/review.md"
```

— is exactly that shape, and `/auto-build` ships one. So reverting the **31st of this phase's own 33 converted sites** left the entire suite green, while `tools/skill_audit_phantom_vars.py` — the worklist this module was written to supersede, and which the phase demoted in the same commit — caught it. I reproduced it before fixing it. Blockquote-ness is now decided by the fence's **opening** line: a `>`-quoted fence is skipped whole, every line of an ordinary fence is scanned. That also reaches three fully-blockquoted fenced regions in `/review-close` carrying 13 lines of live prescribed commands, which had been invisible to *both* scans.

Four more of its findings were real and are fixed: the `$FOO` regex floored names at three characters, hiding `$PR` — **the value `/review-close`'s persistence note is specifically about**, since an empty `gh` operand silently resolves the current branch (the floor existed to dodge one `$X.XX` currency template, now exempted by its exact shape instead); the inline command-word list was hardcoded to five words while `/auto-fix` prescribes in `mkdir` and `cd`; the retired-wording ratchet pinned one literal string, so three paraphrases re-licensed the defect; and `assert "fenced block" in block` was a token check over a 3,322-character note that stayed green when the note was rewritten to say the opposite. Its report also corrected a false sentence I had written in `shape_lib` — "the only sub-floor hit in the corpus is `$X.XX`" — where the true figure is 24 distinct sub-floor names, all but one assigned in-block.

**Two of its findings I checked and did not adopt, with reasons.** The scope objection (the gate reads `core/skills/**` only, so a phantom in `docs/getting-started.md` passes) is real but out of class — those files are not agent-executed, which § 1 of `WORKFLOW.md` states outright, and the second investigation agent had already swept them and found nothing. The nested 4-backtick inversion is a real parser limit, verified to hide nothing today, and is recorded in the worklist rather than fixed.

**Final battery: 57 mutations, 52 killed.** The five survivors are all one-line weakenings *inside a test assertion* — widening an allowlist to a fragment, dropping `tools/` from a population, slicing an offenders list. Closing those in kind needs a test asserting another test's source, which is editable in turn; the recursion terminates at code review, not at a guard. **The one rung that was worth closing is closed:** `git rm tests/test_phantom_shell_vars.py` used to leave the suite green — every vacuity floor that module added lived inside it — so the existence-and-non-vacuity assertion now sits in `test_invocation_shapes.py`, a different file. That was cheaper than the `ENV_PROVIDED` addition the module had called "the cheapest hatch", which is a claim this round falsified.

**Suite: 1971 → 2003 passed + 4 skipped.**

**What this round cost and bought, since Phase 166 left the count open.** Three reviewers, ~610k subagent tokens. The execute lens found the regression I shipped and the live hazard on the path I made reachable; the claims lens found four false statements in prose I wrote this phase and a fifth file in the class; the tests lens found that my own mutation number was measuring the wrong thing and a live site the gate could not see. **Overlap was near zero — each lens's sharpest finding was unique to it**, matching Phase 166's ~15% measurement, and no two lenses would have substituted for each other. On this phase, three was right.

## Phase 170 (executed 2026-07-30 — Wave 1 item 4: the gate that ran before the thing it gated, and the spec that told it to)

Upstream #242, folded with #206. `/review-close` Step 3 resolved the project's `## Pre-merge verification` list and ran it — build, full test suite, lint — while `HEAD` was still `main`, before Step 3b removed a worktree and before Step 4a merged anything. So no approved branch's files were in the working tree and its new tests did not exist. The step is the close's CI gate; it was answering the question about `main`.

**Under `pr` policy it is worse than "the branches are missing."** Step 4-pre cuts the integration branch from *fresh* `origin/main`, so Step 3's tree is not even the base the work will sit on. And the shape the skill itself recommends makes the gate vacuous rather than merely narrow. A `### Ratchet` snippet is defined as filtering `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` — a range that on `main` covers main's local-only commits and nothing else, so **no ratchet snippet has ever run against a feature branch's files**, under either arm. Which arm you get depends on whether `main` has diverged: usually it has, because `/review-close` **manufactures** the divergence (Step 2a's own note: Step 1b commits `review_tasks.md` to `main` before any branch is inspected), and the local-only diff is then a claim flip plus that save — doc-only, so item 4 skips the pass outright. When a prior close already pushed those commits the range is **empty**, every filter short-circuits, and the pass reports green having executed nothing at all. Measured on this repo, whose `main` happened to be level with `origin/main`: zero files. **The round corrected this paragraph** — the first version led with the empty-set arm as though it were the common case, which the skill's own Step 2a note falsifies.

**This is the opposite of Phase 167, and the difference decided the scope.** There, `WORKFLOW.md` § 2.8 and `WORKFLOW_GUIDE.md` had both specified the branch's record all along and only the skill had drifted. Here both specs order verification *before* the merge — § 2.8 step 3 ahead of step 5, and the by-hand Merge Process's "4. Run full verification" ahead of "5. Merge". The skill implements its spec faithfully. **A fix confined to the skill would have left the text that licensed it**, which is the § 8.4-row lesson from Phase 165 in a second place, so all three moved together.

**The fix: Step 3 stays and becomes a declared pre-merge pass; `4a-post` is the gate that counts.** Step 3 keeps the resolution logic — a missing or ambiguous command list still stops the run at the last point where stopping is free — and now says outright that it can only verify the tree it stands on and that nothing in it may be reported as having verified a branch. `4a-post` re-resolves the same list (re-read, not remembered — that is the only way the step can silently run something other than what the consumer declared) and runs it on the merge target.

**Each pass computes its own changed-file list, with one command, on its own tree.** That single substitution is what makes both the doc-only skip and the new surface gate correct in two places instead of needing per-pass arithmetic: `git rev-parse --verify --quiet origin/main >/dev/null && git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD || echo "NO_ORIGIN_MAIN"`. Verified in a scratch repo across all four shapes the skill can be in — on `main` it returns the claim flip alone (`tasks/index.yml`, branch file absent); on an integration branch after cherry-pick + ff-merge it returns the whole assembled diff; on a reused PR branch it returns that branch's own diff; and with no `origin` the bare diff **fatals at exit 128**, which is why the probe is there and why an uncomputable scope gates nothing and skips nothing rather than skipping everything.

**Placement is `after 4a, before 4b` — not the "4c-bis" the filing proposed, and the reason is data loss.** Step 4c deletes each `sysop/runtime/pending-docs/*.md` after routing its content into the shared docs, and those files are **untracked**. A gate failing after 4c would leave that content recoverable only from a commit the run is about to abandon — so verifying the last few doc commits would have been bought with a data-loss window under a failing gate. Before 4b, a stop consumes nothing. The cost is that 4b's and 4c's own commits are outside the gate; they are markdown and YAML written by shipped scripts, and 4c already runs `validate_tasks.py` as its own guard.

**An empty changed-file list means opposite things in the two passes, and that asymmetry is now stated.** At Step 3 it is the normal case and a correct pass. At `4a-post` it is a contradiction — Step 4a just reported merging — so it is a stop: a rebase left a branch a no-op, an ff-merge was skipped after a conflict, or `HEAD` is not the merge target you think it is.

**#206 folded in, as the filing asked.** Each auto-detected command is gated on its own surface appearing in that pass's list, and a surface the diff does not touch is **skipped-not-failed** — the word the reporter asked for, because the point is that the skip is authorized rather than improvised. It is folded rather than deferred because the two are cost-coupled: running the list twice doubles whatever an over-broad auto-detect costs. The gate narrows coverage, so the honesty half ships with it — every changed **code** file no detected surface claims is reported on a new `Unverified surfaces:` line rather than disappearing, and the escape is named: a consumer-authored `## Pre-merge verification` section is never surface-gated.

**The filing's own rationale is false against this tree, and the truth is worse.** #242 argues the wrong-tree green matters "because the green is recorded in the PR body as evidence." It is not: the only `--body` this skill writes is a fixed string, no commit message carries a verification result, and Step 8's report template had **no verification line at all**. The green was recorded *nowhere* — unauditable rather than misfiled — which is why the fix adds `Verification:` and `Unverified surfaces:` lines. Phase 158's precedent applies: a gate whose skips nobody can see is not a fix.

**The regression this phase nearly shipped was in Step 3c.** Its skip read "If Step 3 was skipped (doc-only diff), skip Step 3c too." After the fix Step 3 doc-only-skips on nearly every cycle — main's local-only diff is a claim flip plus a `review_tasks.md` save — so that coupling would have disabled the manual-smoke gate almost always, on runs whose branches carried real code. It now keys on the whole run being doc-only, checked per approved branch. The miss it would have caused is a human never being asked.

**Three loose ends reconciled rather than left.** `_shared/main-push-guard.md` Rule B already prescribed a second execution of the same list when a rebase changes the base — it named Step 3, the one pass whose tree is not what moved, and now names `4a-post`. `/claim-task` Step 7b and `/auto-build` Step 4b both told the reader `/review-close` covers them "at merge time" — a claim that was false before this phase and is a division of labour after it, so both now say which step and that a worktree gate is the only thing that verifies a branch in isolation. And `--dry-run` says explicitly that `4a-post` cannot run under it, because Step 3's green standing in for the merged gate is the exact substitution the split exists to remove.

**Author-side pass, reported per Phase 166's rule.** Rule 3 (run the prescribed commands): the two new fenced blocks were **extracted verbatim from the shipped file and executed**, not retyped — the scope command in both passes, and the clean-tree probe in three states (clean → `CLEAN`; a formatter rewriting a tracked file → `DIRTY`; untracked build artifacts only → `CLEAN`, which is the claim the prose makes about `git diff` not seeing untracked files). Rule 2 (re-read new prose against the code): this is where the `4c-bis`-vs-`4a-post` placement changed, and where Step 3c's coupling was caught. Rule 1 (mutate the guard's assumptions, not just its content): **the first 26 mutations were all reverts of text I had just written, and adding five assumption-mutations found a real hole** — `check_both_passes_share_one_scope_command` tested a *substring*, so fencing the block as ```` ```text ```` and prefixing the command with `#` left it green: a commented-out command was marking the pass compliant. It now resolves from executable fenced lines. Final battery **31/31**.
